Darth Vader gives Area Manager, right? (there's a longer version of this review, with more about my luckless adolescent career in the British civil service, but you'll have to go over to Substack to read that.) In my youth I worked for a while in the UK civil service. I wasn't the most hard-working or conscientious civil servant in that particular branch office of Her Majesty's Land Registry. In fact, during one episode of striking negligence and work-avoidance, there was an encounter with an Area Manager that, to this day, sends a shiver down my spine. What brought this to mind in watching the first and second movies in the original Star Wars sequence was Darth Vader’s striking Area Manager vibe. In The Empire Strikes Back he’s supposed to be the Empire’s most terrifying entity, a fearsome knight, damaged beyond pity (and somehow endowed with extra Force not available to others), a warrior but also evidently a man smart enough to slink away from the Death Star before the rebels blew it up. Vader’s spaceship in this episode is imaginatively called the Executor. The Death Star is gone but the Empire is back on the front foot. We wonder, was the destruction of its super-weapon actually an existential crisis for the Empire or did the rebels really just blow up a pointless, bloated boondoggle, somebody’s vanity project? Was the Imperial leadership secretly happy that this stupid, monolithic, over-budget piece of shit was atomised by the hippy retards from the rebellion? It’s his flagship but Vader's not actually the boss. He walks the decks with that awkward ‘I don’t actually work here but I could cause you pain’ authority. He drops in and throws his weight around. Near the beginning of this film he literally kills the ship’s commander - an Admiral with the perfectly Star Wars name Kendal Ozzel - for some tactical snafu (of course, the lore tells us that Ozzel is an over-promoted Imperial civil servant who deserved it anyway so that makes sense). On the ship Vader can do what he wants. He cruises around looking purposeful but obviously not 100% across the layout here. He’s allowed to use the service lift if he wants to but you can tell he doesn’t really know how to, so someone has to show him. The coffee machine in the staff lounge is beyond him and, although the toilets are in the same place on every deck, he can never find the VIP bathroom. In more recent Star Wars expressions - guerrilla war drama Andor, for instance - the Empire’s bureaucracy is fleshed out a bit. We learn more about its essentially colonial-extractive economics, we get some detail about policing (George Orwell the colonial police officer would have recognised these methods). At this point, though, two movies into the original sequence, Lucas’s Empire is still incomplete: a non-specific polity vaguely modelled on - what? Leopold’s Belgian Empire? Britain in India? Stalin’s Soviet Union? We know it’s brutal, arbitrary and acquisitive but we don’t get an org chart or a five-year plan. Vader’s status is essentially that of colonial enforcer. He’s not in charge (that’s the Emperor obvs) and he may not even be on the management committee. Strategy’s not his thing and he’s certainly not a figurehead. He’s important but he’s not a world-historical figure, despite his status in a state that spans a galaxy. Space Hegel would not have swooned and called Vader ‘the world-spirit in a tie fighter’. What Hegel thought he saw in Napoleon; his will to change everything, to overturn the old order and replace it with pure rationality, is not present here. And this obviously makes Vader, well, uninteresting. The history of the galaxy does not pass through him, he will not be remembered as anything other than a brute. To the Emperor’s Stalin he is not Trotsky but Beria. I’m no expert but I assume this explains the whole Sith situation - setting up a parallel regime in the shadowy, immaterial realm of The Force. It’s an effort to give Vader a more consequential role - beyond workplace bullying and brutalising the natives. Movies don’t need world-historical villains, of course. One-dimensional brutes are fine. But when a film aspires to importance, when we feel its creators are telling us something about the world - about power, dominion, government, family, society and so on - we need to believe that our villains have historical stature, even when they are not real. Kurtz, Lime, Corleone: all convince us that they sit at a critical juncture or that they will alter the direction of the larger storyline. It’s harder with science fiction, because there’s no historical context against which to set this villain and their villainy. But it’s not impossible. Bradbury, Herbert, Le Guin; Tarkovsky, Scott, Kubrick, all give us future villains who aspire to alter their timelines, leave a trace, beyond cruelty and domination. Operators who do more than enforce the plan. You’re going to have to forgive me for being prissy about this big, trashy, treasured entertainment brand but this is ultimately the weakness of The Empire Strikes Back and of the whole Star Wars franchise: this dumb, unmotivated conflict. This Empire: a vast, galaxy-wide enterprise, presumably built across centuries and at unimaginable cost - to those building it and to those who came up against it - apparently cares only about domination. And its necessary antagonist - its antithesis - the rebels, only care about opposing it. Neither apparently owns a positive vision for their world or for their people.

Wow, this might be the most overrated movie of all time. Beyond the visual spectacle and that classic score, there is almost nothing good here. In my previous review, I talked about the first Star Wars from 1977 and said that it was kinda good but had its problems. In this movie, those same problems return, but multiplied to the point where they fill the entire film. Things just keep happening and happening without any good construction or writing behind them. The relationships between the characters, my God, only get worse in terms of superficiality. It is painfully cringe-worthy to watch the forced romance between Han Solo and Princess Leia. The movie seems to imply that she, as a woman character, necessarily has to have a romance with one of the protagonists in order to be relevant in the film, because the plot keeps forcing this every time she appear, even when it doesn't make any sense. As I already pointed out in my previous review, her character is poorly written, and in this movie it only gets worse. The only character I genuinely liked in the first movie was Han Solo, and even they managed to ruin him here. Not even Harrison Ford could save it. The screenplay is so bad that it actually hurts. The dialogue sounds like it was written by a child. In fact, this entire movie feels like it came straight out of a story created by a child with an extremely vivid imagination. At one point, I just kept watching to see if it would remain this bad until the end, but I had absolutely no interest in what was happening, because this movie never managed to spark any in me. Finishing it was a struggle. The feeling I get is that all the visual spectacle and action scenes every five minutes are here to hide the superficiality and poor writing of the film. It keeps people engaged with explosions, gunfights, and spaceship chases. And judging by what people say about this movie, it seems to have worked. I genuinely don’t understand what people see as being so great here. I said I thought the first one already had problems, but I never imagined the second could be this bad, especially considering the acclaim it receives, which is even greater than the first film’s. And another thing: the performances are terrible. The material given to the actors isn’t good, and they didn’t have much to work with, since the writing of the characters is one of the worst aspects of this movie. But for God’s sake, the actor playing Luke Skywalker and the actress playing Princess Leia are absolutely dreadful. That probably explains why neither of them managed to land many significant roles outside the Star Wars saga. They aren’t the only terrible performances here, but I highlight them because they are playing the primary characters. In the end, the only memorable moments are the final sequence and the famous scene where Darth Vader reveals that he is Luke Skywalker’s father. Other than that, it is a pretty forgettable and overrated movie. Maybe this was the starting point for the culture of superficial blockbusters we see today, like superhero movies, for example. Films that use and abuse visual spectacle to hide their poor writing. I can say that Star Wars walked so Marvel could run. I was going to watch the entire original trilogy for the first time, but after this, I’m giving up. If this is supposed to be the best movie in the whole Star Wars franchise, I don’t even wanna know what the worst one is.

There’s always something so interesting and admittedly greedy when a writer/director see their movie do so well, they feel the need to make a sequel to capitalize on the success. Lucas himself was even half in and half out on it considering he gave the directing responsibilities to someone else. I think what made Star Wars work especially well is that they went into Empire seemingly planning on making a third as well. So this one allowed characters to breathe and explore other relationships. Luke spends all of maybe 5 minutes or so of screen time with everyone. He’s off getting lost, he’s healing, he’s being a pilot, then he’s with Yoda for a third of the film, then it’s the final battle. Hell they even split up R2 and 3P0 in this movie. They definitely went in with a few things in mind they wanted to get done. Get Luke started on being a Jedi, build up Han and Leia’s relationship (that part they could’ve done better imo), and make sure Vader is as intimidating and power housing as possible. And for the most part I think they did that very well. As for the twist, it’s so legendary. I’m pretty sure even before watching, I knew he was his dad. To be able to experience that for the first time would be legendary to see. I do like this movie a lot. I will say I do think I still like A New Hope just a little more. Mostly for it being a completed story and for seeing our group in action together. I love Yoda, I love Lando, our new characters add so much to the story and the franchise as a whole. Luke vs Vader is phenomenal from an emotionally aspect, yea not much else to add honestly.

The Empire Strikes Back ★★★★★ The Empire Strikes Back is one of the most perfect middle chapters in a trilogy ever created, and one of the best films ever made. As a kid, this absolutely blew me away. This was the Star Wars movie I would rent the most from the video store growing up, and returning to it now, it is easy to understand why it had such a hold on me. The story picks up with the Rebel Alliance hiding out on the frozen planet Hoth while the Empire searches for them. After the Rebels are attacked, Luke Skywalker begins a journey of Jedi training under the mysterious Yoda, while Han Solo, Princess Leia and Chewbacca attempt to escape Imperial forces. Their paths eventually lead them to Cloud City, where Darth Vader is waiting. The film expands the Star Wars universe considerably while giving its characters much more depth and putting them through some genuinely difficult situations. What makes Empire so remarkable is how much darker and more mature it feels than the original without losing the adventure and wonder that made Star Wars special. The Battle of Hoth remains one of the greatest action sequences in science-fiction, the introduction of Yoda is unforgettable, and the Millennium Falcon’s escape from the Empire is pure cinematic fun. Then there is the relationship between Han and Leia, which gives the movie an emotional center that balances all the spectacle. The film was directed by Irvin Kershner rather than George Lucas, who remained heavily involved as the creator and producer. Leigh Brackett and Lawrence Kasdan worked on the screenplay alongside Lucas. Lucas chose not to direct because he was simultaneously building Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic, and the production ultimately became considerably more expensive and complicated than originally anticipated. The Hoth sequences were particularly brutal to make. The production traveled to Finse, Norway, where the crew dealt with temperatures approaching -30°C, heavy snowstorms and high winds. Some of the footage was shot only a few feet from the hotel because the weather made traveling farther nearly impossible. Fortunately, none of that misery shows on screen. It looks like another galaxy instead of a film crew wondering whether their fingers still work. The film opened on May 21, 1980, beginning its 70mm run in just 41 theaters across 16 cities before expanding. It had an $18 million production budget and earned $209,398,025 domestically during its original release. Later releases brought its domestic total to $292,753,960, while its worldwide total across releases reached $550,016,086. The original release also had an unusual box-office rollout by modern standards. It opened in a relatively small number of theaters, then expanded dramatically, reaching 1,278 theaters during its run. By the time it went wide, it was absolutely dominating the box office. Perhaps the greatest compliment that can be paid to The Empire Strikes Back is that it doesn’t feel like a movie designed simply to get audiences from the first film to the third. It stands completely on its own. The characters evolve, the universe gets larger, the stakes become more personal, and the filmmaking remains spectacular more than four decades later. Final Verdict The Empire Strikes Back is pretty much the gold standard for how to make the middle chapter of a trilogy. It expanded everything that worked about the original Star Wars, made the characters richer, delivered some unforgettable action and somehow managed to make the galaxy feel considerably bigger. For a movie that is essentially the middle piece of a larger story, it feels remarkably complete. Some sequels improve on their predecessors. This one helped define what a great sequel could be.

Empire Strikes Back didn’t just make the galaxy bigger, it made it deeper. It takes the adventure from A New Hope and gives it so much weight. Suddenly the galaxy now feels colder, darker, larger, and more complex.
The perfect sequel.

It has arguably the most iconic fight scene of all time, and that entire confrontation between Luke and Vader is cinema history at its absolute peak. The tension, the visuals, the sound design, the reveal, everything just lands. “I am your father” is one of those moments so deeply ingrained in pop culture that whenever those words are said, it’s recognised everywhere. As big of a reveal as "I am your father" is, I don't think it hits as perfectly as it does without Mark Hamill's absolutely perfect reaction of shock and pure horror. “No like, I am your father” 2 hours of true cinematic greatness. This will forever be my favourite Star Wars film and there’s a reason it’s more often or not viewed as the best film. It’s just so great. The way this film presents the enemy is so incredible the “imperial march” soundtrack will always haunt me as I used to be terrified of Darth Vader as a kid and for good reason ! He is truly the figure head of this movie alongside Luke Skywalker. Every frame either of them are in just feels so important so poignant. They are involved in 3 all time scenes 3 of the best scenes not only in Star Wars history but in cinematic history aswell. The scene in degobah when he comes out from round the corner and we think we finally have this duel this duel of fates that we’ve been waiting for. It’s so scary to see Darth Vader in action like that, the way the camera moves and goes in and out of slow motion is genius. The first real fight on bespin is perhaps the best fight in the entire series, so quiet and restrained, Vader using his experience and his knowledge and Luke in contrast using confidence and sheer power at times to keep himself a float. It’s an unbelievable fight that lasts almost 10 minutes and 3 different sets! And of course who could forgot “no I am your father” one of the most influential moments in history one of the biggest plot twists in cinematic history and an absolute masterpiece in directing and story telling. The lead up to this is absolutely insane and I can imagine watching this in cinemas in the 80s not having a clue what’s about to come, I remember being shocked when I first watched it so watching it in the cinemas must have been a experience of a lifetime. The reaction from Luke the speech after from Vader it’s truly one of the best moments in the history of cinema, goosebumps every-time. Away from that we have so much more good in this film, Han and Leia were a great choice and whenever and whoever decided to have them 2 together should get a reward because there meant for each other. The back in forth they have throughout the whole first act makes the eventual pay off so worth it. Yoda is introduced as this scrawny almost annoying little green man but eventually his influence on the film becomes apparent, the whole degobah sequence is great. The introduction of the emperor is one of my favourite things as they present him in a way where we see Lord Vader bowing down and following orders from him. Standing over him speaking about the force and conveying that this is anakins son makes him seem and sound so powerful more powerful that anyone else, so harrowing in the way he speaks signifying to the audience that no matter how powerful Vader is he is the man in charge… absolutely mythical filmmaking. The sets, the cinematography, the soundtrack, the world building it’s all there in this film and to think it came out in 1980 is just absurd. It’s one of the greatest films of all time and will continue to stand the test of time for a very very long time. What a name aswell “the empire strikes back” fucking sick !
